text: Welcome! Before we play, let's get you sitting well, with soft round hands. Then you'll make your very first music on the black keys.

Let's get set before we play. Sit on the front half of the bench, in the middle of the piano. Your arms are level with the keys and your feet are flat on the floor. Shoulders down, sit tall, and breathe.
Let your arms hang down loose. Now lift your hands up to the keys, but keep that same soft shape. Round fingers, like holding a ball. That is your piano hand.

Put your thumb behind your middle finger to help it. Now let your whole arm drop into a black key, like a heavy feather, then float back up. Drop, and let go. The sound comes from weight, not from pushing.
Black keys sound nice in any order, so you can make music already! Low keys sound like a big bear. High keys sound like a little bird. Play low, then high, and listen.

Let's meet the keyboard. You'll find the groups of black keys, and the most important note of all, middle C.

Before we play, let's sit nicely. Sit in the middle of the piano, with your arms level with the keys. Make your fingers round, like you are holding a little ball. If your hands feel tight, shake them out and try again.
Look at the black keys. They come in little groups, two together, then three together, again and again. This pattern is like a map. It helps you find any key on the piano.
Find a group of two black keys. The white key just to the left of them is called C. The C in the middle of the piano is called middle C. It is our home base. Listen.
Every finger has a number. Your thumb is one, then two, three, four, and your little finger is five. Now put your right thumb on middle C and let it sink gently into the key.
Going to the right makes the sound go higher, like a bird. Going to the left makes it lower, like a bear. Listen, low, middle, high.
Next up, Play middle C four times. Locate middle C reliably and play it with right hand finger 1. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Music only uses seven letters, A, B, C, D, E, F, G. Then they start again. From C we go C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and then C again.
Here are some easy landmarks. D sits between the two black keys. E is just to the right of them. F is just to the left of the three black keys. G is next to F.
Put your right thumb on middle C. Let your other fingers rest on D, E, F and G, one finger on each key. This is called C position. Listen to it go up and down.

Time for the black keys. You'll learn that a sharp is the key just to the right, and play your first sharps.
A sharp means one key higher, to the right. The black key just right of C is called C sharp. The black key just right of F is F sharp.
In the group of two black keys we have C sharp and D sharp. In the group of three we have F sharp, G sharp and A sharp.

Music has a heartbeat, called the pulse. Let's feel it, count it, and play right on it.
Music has a steady beat, like your heartbeat. You will hear four clicks to get ready. Then play middle C right on each click. Tick, tick, tick, tick.
This note, with a filled-in head and a stick, is a quarter note. It lasts one beat. Count out loud, one, two, three, four.

Let's read some music! You'll learn the treble staff, and play C to G just by reading the notes.
Music is written on five lines, called the staff. The higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. This curly sign is the treble clef. It shows us where G lives.
Middle C sits on its own little line under the staff. Each step up on the staff is the next white key to the right, C, D, E, F, G. Line, space, line, space.

Some notes are long and some are short. Today you'll hold half notes and whole notes for just the right time.
Some notes last longer. A half note is hollow with a stick, and lasts two beats. A whole note is hollow with no stick, and lasts four beats. Keep the key down while you count.
Listen to the difference, C for one beat, D for two beats, and E for four beats.

Rhythms have words you can say out loud. Say them, clap them, then play them. You'll also learn the words that tell you how fast to go.
Rhythms have words. Say tah for one beat. tah-ah for two beats. tah-ah-ah for three, and tah-ah-ah-ah for four. A rest is a quiet shush. Say the words and your hands will follow.
Count the numbers too, one, two, three, four, in every bar. Clap and say the rhythm words while you count. When they line up, your rhythm is right.
Some words tell you how fast to play. They are Italian. Adagio is slow. Andante is walking speed. Allegro is quick and happy. Presto is super fast.
Next up, Say the rhythm. Hear four beats and pick the syllables that match. Listen, then pick your answer.
Next up, Play and say it. Play while saying tah tah tah-ah, tah-ah tah-ah, tah shush tah shush, tah-ah-ah-ah. Press start. You will hear a count in, then play along with the click.

Low notes are written on the bass staff. Its sign has two dots, and they hug the line called F. Your left hand usually plays these low notes.
Now the left hand. Put your little finger, number five, on the C below middle C. The other fingers rest on D, E, F and G. Your thumb ends up on G.

Here's a reading shortcut. Learn three landmark notes, then find every other note by stepping and skipping from them.
Learn three landmark notes. Treble G, the treble clef curls around its line. Bass F, the bass clef's two dots sit on either side of its line. Middle C, on its own little line between the staves.
A step goes from a line to the very next space, or a space to the next line. On the piano, that's the very next white key. One step up from G is A.
A skip goes from a line to the next line, jumping over one key. One skip up from G is B. Look which way the notes go and how far, and your finger will find it.
Next up, Name it from the landmark, treble. Notes near treble G. Listen, then pick your answer.
Next up, Name it from the landmark, bass. Notes near bass F. Listen, then pick your answer.
Next up, The whole staff. Any note on the treble or bass staff, plus ledger lines. Listen, then pick your answer.

Next up, Steps and skips from F. Left hand, reading from bass F. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
Your first real melody! You'll play the famous Ode to Joy, slowly and in time.
Here is your first real tune! It is called Ode to Joy, by Beethoven. It only uses C position, and the notes mostly move to the key right next door. Listen and follow along.
Next up, Notes first wait mode. Learn both phrases without time pressure. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Two notes at once, then three. Today you'll play your very first chords.
Now let's press two keys at the same time, so they make one sound together. Try C and E. Then try C and G. Press them exactly together.
Add one more note in the middle, C, E and G together. That is a chord, the C major chord. It sounds happy and settled, like home. Use fingers one, three and five.
The same hand shape works in other places. Here is F major, and here is G major. Listen to C, then F, then G, and back home to C.
The app listens for every note in the chord. If one is missing, it will tell you which one. Listen to how full it sounds when the left hand adds a low C.

Let's make every finger strong and independent, so each one plays clearly on its own.
Keep your hand quiet and still, and let only one finger move at a time. The other fingers just rest on their keys. If a finger tags along by itself, slow down. That is what we are training.
Lift each finger from the big knuckle, where your finger joins your hand. Keep the fingertip firm. Try to make every note equally loud.

Your thumb learns a new trick today, tucking under, so you can play a whole scale smoothly.
Here is a magic trick for playing more than five notes. Play C, D, E with fingers one, two, three. Then slide your thumb under your hand to play F. Now keep going up. Listen.
Coming down, your middle finger crosses over your thumb. Get your thumb ready early, so there is no gap in the sound.

Short and bouncy, then rolling and smooth. You'll learn staccato and broken chords with the right hand.
A little dot over a note means play it short and bouncy, like touching something hot. Let the key spring right back up. This is called staccato.
C, E, G played one after another is a broken chord. Keep your hand shaped over all three keys, so each finger is ready.
Next up, Staccato C, E, G. Short notes eighth note and rest in time at 72 beats per minute. Press start. You will hear a count in, then play along with the click.

Let's give your left hand jobs to do, simple patterns that sit under a tune.
This left-hand pattern goes low, high, middle, high, C, G, E, G. It is called Alberti bass. Mozart used it a lot. Keep the thumb light. Listen.
This is a waltz pattern. Play one low note, then two soft chords, oom, pah, pah. Lean a little on the oom.
Next up, Alberti bass C, G, C. Eighth notes at 63 beats per minute, fingers five, one, three, one. Press start. You will hear a count in, then play along with the click.

Two staves joined together make the grand staff. It's how piano music is written, and today you'll read it.
Piano music uses two staffs joined together. The top one is mostly for the right hand, the bottom one for the left hand. Middle C sits right between them.
Here is an easy rule. Notes on the top staff are for your right hand. Notes on the bottom staff are for your left hand. Check which staff first.
Next up, Middle C from both sides. Alternate right hand C finger 1 and left hand C finger 1 reading the grand staff. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Both hands together, moving the same way, then moving in opposite directions, like a mirror.
Both hands moving the same way is called parallel motion. Your right hand starts with the thumb, your left hand with the little finger. Up they go, together.
Now the hands move away from each other, like opening a book. Both thumbs start on middle C. This is called contrary motion. It feels natural, because the finger numbers match.
Next up, Parallel five-finger. C D E F G in both hands together, an octave apart. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Your left hand can play small chords too, C, F and G. These shapes only move a tiny bit, so soon you will not even need to look.
Change the chord on beat one, exactly with the tune. Practice the left hand alone first, then add the right hand slowly.

Let's play two notes at once in the right hand, a third apart. The top note sings the tune, the lower note sings along.
In choir songs, the right hand often plays two singers at once, the tune on top, and a helper part just below it. Most often they are a third apart. That means you skip one white key. Listen.
For thirds, use fingers one and three, then two and four, then three and five, as you climb. Keep your hand still, and press both keys at exactly the same moment.
The tune is on top. Lean a tiny bit more on your top finger, so the tune sings a little louder than the helper part. Listen to the difference.
If you hear two clicks instead of one sound, the notes are not together yet. Go slowly. Play each pair, stop, check, then move on.
Next up, Thirds up and down. C and E to G and B and back, fingers one, three, two, four, three, five. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Wider pairs today, sixths, and a mix of shapes, still in the right hand.
A sixth is a wider pair, like C up to A. Use your thumb and little finger. Sixths sound warm and open. Listen.
A real helper part does not stay the same distance below the tune. It moves to the nearest good note, so the gap keeps changing. Watch both notes in every pair.
In sixths your thumb plays the lower note. Keep it light, and keep your top fingers round, so the tune stays smooth.
Next up, Sixths up and down. C and A to G and E and back, fingers 1 and 5. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
Next up, 3rds to 6ths. Alternate a third and a sixth on each step. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.

Now the left hand plays two notes together, including a bouncy shuffle.
Now the left hand plays two notes, the bottom note and the note five keys up. Use your little finger and your thumb. This sound is the backbone of rock and folk music. Listen.
Keep your little finger on C, and rock your top finger between G and A, G, A, G, A. This is the shuffle, the left hand of lots of blues and rock and roll songs. Listen.
In choir music, the left hand plays two singers at once, the tenor and the bass. Read both notes on the bottom staff and press them together.

Four voices, two in each hand, just like a little choir under your fingers.
A hymn has four singers written on two staffs. The right hand plays the top two, the soprano and the alto. The left hand plays the bottom two, the tenor and the bass. Listen.
Read from the bottom up. Find the lowest note first, it tells you the chord. Then the top note, that is the tune. Then fill in the middle.
If a note stays the same in the next chord, keep that finger down and only move the others. It sounds smooth, just like a choir.

Eighth notes are quicker, two in every beat. Say tee tee and play them evenly.
An eighth note lasts half a beat, so two of them fit into one beat. They are joined by a little bar on top. Count, one and two and three and four and.
The beat stays the same speed. Eighth notes just fit two notes into each beat. Most people rush them, so count out loud and follow the clicks.

A dot makes a note longer. Today you'll play dotted rhythms with a little lilt.
A dot after a note makes it longer, by half again. A dotted half note lasts three beats. A dotted quarter is often followed by a short note, long, short.
A dotted rhythm sounds like taaa-ti. You can hear it in Ode to Joy. Feel the long note, then the quick one.

Silence is music too. Let's count through the rests and come back in on time.
A rest means silence. Every note has a matching rest. During a rest, lift your hand, but keep counting in your head.
The most common mistake is coming in too early after a rest. Say the silent beats out loud, quietly, one, two, three, four.

Swing makes jazz feel like jazz. Long, short, long, short.

Jazz players often play the next chord a little early, just before the beat. This push makes the music lean forward and feel exciting.

Two, five, one is the most important move in jazz. Let's follow the guide tones.
The two, five, one is jazz's favorite little sentence. Two gets ready. Five builds tension. One brings it home. Listen.
Jazz pianists often play just two notes in the left hand, the bottom note and one color note. This is called a shell. It is simple, and it sounds great. Listen.
Watch the color notes from chord to chord. They only move a tiny bit, or stay the same. If you play just these, people can still hear the chords. Listen and compare.

The blues, its twelve-bar form, its scale, and how to phrase it.
The blues is twelve bars long, and it repeats. It uses bluesy seventh chords all the way through. Count the bars as you listen. Listen.
The blues scale has six notes that make anything sound bluesy. One note in the middle is extra special. Slide through it, do not stop on it. Listen.
A piano can't bend notes like a guitar, so we crush them. Play two neighbor keys almost together, sliding off the first one. It sounds like a singer's bluesy slide. Listen.
Blues phrases talk to each other. Play a short idea, like a question. Leave a little space. Then answer it. Space is just as important as notes.

Let's start improvising, using chord tones and notes that lead into them.
To make up a jazz tune that fits, land on a chord note on the strong beats. Those notes always sound right. Listen.
Here is a jazz trick. Play the key right below your target note, just before it. That tiny bit of tension makes the target sound great. Listen.
Another trick, surround your target. Play the note above it, then the note below it, then land on it. Listen.
Start with a tiny idea of three to five notes. Repeat it, then change it a little. Good solos tell a story from one small idea.

A walking bass in the left hand, chords in the right. Two-hand jazz piano.
A walking bass plays one note on every beat. Beat one is the chord's name note. Beats two and three are chord notes or neighbors. Beat four leads into the next chord. Listen.
Sneaking in from the key right next door makes the next chord sound like it had to happen. That is the walking bass player's secret.
While the left hand walks, the right hand plays short, light chords. Keep them gentle, so the bass line can breathe.

Two different chords, G seven and D flat seven, share the same important notes. So jazz players swap one for the other. The bass then slides down smoothly. Listen and compare.

A lead sheet only shows the tune and the chord names. You decide how to play the rest. This is how jazz musicians read songs.
Start simple. Right hand plays the tune, with swing. Left hand plays a simple shell on each chord. Add more when that feels easy.

Four voices, soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Let's learn their ranges and spacing.
Choirs sing in four parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Each part is its own little tune. Together they make the harmony. Listen.
Each voice has notes it can sing comfortably. Sopranos sing high, basses sing low. Keep each part in its comfortable zone, so nobody strains. Listen.
Keep the top three voices close together, no more than an octave apart. The bass can be further away. And voices should not cross over each other. Listen and compare.
A chord has three notes, but a choir has four voices, so one note is sung twice. Usually we double the bottom note of the chord. Never leave out the middle note. Listen and compare.

Good voice leading makes every part easy to sing. Here are the rules.
If two chords share a note, let the same voice keep singing it. It sounds smooth, and it is easy to sing. Listen.
Each voice moves to the closest note of the next chord. Small steps are easy to sing. Leave the big jumps to the bass. Listen and compare.
When the bass goes up, let the other voices go down, and the other way round. It keeps every part independent and interesting. Listen.
Two voices should not move together in fifths or octaves. It makes two singers sound like one, and the music sounds empty. Listen to the wrong way, then the right way.
Some notes really want to move. The note just below home wants to step up to home. Follow these pulls and your endings will sound strong. Listen.

Cadences are how phrases end, like commas and full stops in music.
The perfect cadence is a full stop. The five chord goes to the one chord, and the music sounds finished. Listen.
The plagal cadence sounds like the Amen at the end of a hymn. Four goes to one. It is soft and peaceful. Listen.
A half cadence is like a comma. The music stops on the five chord, and you feel there is more to come. Listen.
A deceptive cadence is a surprise. You expect home, but you land on the sad six chord instead. Listen to the difference.
A song often asks a question, then answers it. The first line ends with a comma, and the second line ends with a full stop. Plan these endings first.

Inversions give the bass a smooth line that's easy to sing.
Put a different chord note in the bass, and the chord sounds lighter. It also lets the bass walk smoothly instead of jumping. Listen and compare.

Let's harmonize a melody, one step at a time.
To add harmony to a tune, start with the endings. If a line ends on the home note, end it with a full stop. If not, end it with a comma.
Every tune note fits in a few different chords. Pick a chord for the important notes, the ones on the strong beats. Listen to the choices.
Chords like to travel in a circle, home, then away, then tension, then back home. Change chords once or twice a bar, and keep it steady.
Make the bass a second tune. When the top goes up, let the bass go down. Step where you can, and use the chord's name note at the endings.

Passing notes, neighbour notes and suspensions make the parts move beautifully.
A passing note fills the gap between two chord notes, step by step. It makes the line flow, without changing the chord. Listen and compare.
A neighbor note steps away and comes right back, like a little decoration.
A suspension holds a note from the last chord for a moment, then lets it fall to where it belongs. It sounds tender and beautiful. Listen and compare.

Different ways to accompany on the piano, from simple to rich.
An arrangement keeps the same chords, but changes how they are played. Blocks sound like a hymn. Broken chords sound like a ballad. Listen.
For slow songs, play a low note, then spread the chord upwards, one note at a time. Use the pedal to let it ring. Listen.
Stride piano jumps, a low note on beats one and three, a chord in the middle on beats two and four. It is the sound of old ragtime piano. Listen.
For pop songs, the left hand plays simple low notes, and the right hand plays chords in a bouncy rhythm. Leave space for the singer.

Now arrange a whole song for choir.
To arrange a song for a choir, you need the tune and the chords. You can work them out by ear, or sing the tune into Sing to score.
Put the tune where the sopranos can sing it comfortably. If it is too low, give the tune to the tenors instead, and add harmony around it.
Do not use all four parts the whole time. Start with everyone singing the tune together, add a harmony part, then save the full four parts for the chorus.
The sopranos sing the tune. The bass makes a good low line. The alto and tenor fill in with the closest notes. Then sing each part alone to check it.

Welcome, church musician! We start with two parts of a hymn, the tune and the bass.

A hymn has four singers written on two lines of music. On top, soprano sings the tune, and alto sings under it. On the bottom, tenor, and bass, the lowest. Your right hand plays the top two. Your left hand plays the bottom two.
Start with the outside parts, the tune on top and the bass at the bottom. Those two together already sound full enough for people to sing with. Learn each hand alone first, then put them together.
This tune is called Old Hundredth. It is more than four hundred and fifty years old, and churches all over the world sing it. Every note is one beat. At the end of each line, everyone takes a breath.

When the tune moves but the alto stays, keep the alto key held down. Don't let it go early, or the hymn sounds thin.
Amazing Grace has three beats in a bar, like a gentle waltz. It starts on beat three. Count three, then one two three, one two three, and lean softly on each one.

The tenor joins your left hand, and you play the full four-part hymn.

Read each beat as one chord shape, from the bottom up, bass, tenor, alto, soprano. Your eyes see the shape, and your hands move there in one go. Go slowly, one hand at a time, then together.

Three honest ways to make a hard hymn playable, so you're ready for Sunday.
When a hymn is too hard, keep what the singers need most, the tune, a steady beat, and the right chords. The middle notes are extra. Make it simpler until you can play it well.
The first easy way, play just the tune and the bass. It is clear, simple, and always right.
The second easy way, your right hand plays the tune. Your left hand holds two notes of the chord, the root and the fifth, for the whole bar.
The third way, your right hand plays full chords on every beat, and your left hand plays the bass in big octaves. This sounds strong for a big room full of people.

Introductions, a singable tempo, fermatas, and the Amen. Let's lead with confidence.
Before people sing, play the last line of the hymn as an introduction. It tells them the tune, the starting note, and how fast to go. Then breathe together and begin.
Pick a speed where one breath lasts a whole line. Too slow, and people run out of air. Too fast, and the words get jumbled. Sing the words quietly to yourself while you play.
A fermata at the end of a line means hold and breathe. Hold the chord a little longer, lift your hands, and come back in together on the next line.
Many hymns end with Amen, sung on two chords, chord four, then chord one. It's called the church cadence. Play it slowly and warmly.
Next up, Amen in four keys. four to I in C, G, F and D. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
Next up, Play the introduction. The last line of Old Hundredth in four parts, in time, at singing speed. Press start. You will hear a count in, then play along with the click.
You're the leader now. Keep the beat steady and breathe with the people.
Everyone follows the piano, so keep your beat steady, even if the singing slows down. Play the tune and the bass a little louder than the middle notes.
At the end of each line, lift the last chord a tiny bit early so everyone can breathe. Then come back in right on the beat. The beat never stops.
Play softer when the words are gentle, and fuller when they are joyful. On the last verse, add a low bass note for a big finish. Between verses, keep the beat going.

Letters above the music tell you the chords. Let's read them and play them right away.

Chord symbols are letters above the music. A letter on its own, like G, means a major chord. A small m, like E m, means minor. A seven adds one more note. A slash tells you which note goes in the bass.
Every key has a family of chords. Chords one, four, and five are major. Chords two, three, and six are minor. In the key of G, the family is G, A minor, B minor, C, D, and E minor.
Don't jump around for every chord. Keep your right hand near middle C and move each finger to the closest note of the next chord. Your left hand plays the root, the chord's main note.

Make the most of a keyboard or an organ, voices, styles, split, and smooth organ playing.
On a keyboard, the voice button picks the sound, like piano or organ. The style button adds drums and a band, so keep it soft in church. Split gives your left hand a different sound, like a bass.
Transpose moves everything up or down, so you can play in an easy key. It is handy, but learn the real keys too. When the keyboard is off, what you know stays with you.
Some keyboards play a whole chord when you press one key. It helps at the start, but it can guess wrong. Learn to play the chords yourself as soon as you can.
On an organ, the sound stops the moment you let go. So hold every note for its full length, and join it smoothly to the next one. If two chords share a note, just keep holding it.
On an organ, start with a soft, normal sound, called an eight-foot stop. Add a four-foot stop to make it brighter. Your feet play the bass on the pedals, so your left hand only plays the tenor.

Four chords, a thousand songs. Let's give them a real groove.
Four chords make thousands of songs, C, G, A minor, and F. Keep your right hand close, moving only a little between chords. Your left hand plays the main note of each chord.
Now add a groove. Play long, long, short, on one, on the and of two, and on four. Count one, two and, three, four. That's the heartbeat of pop music.
For lots of energy, play the low note in octaves on every beat. For a gentle song, just hold the low note for the whole bar.

Small changes to a chord make big colours. Sus, add two, six, and augmented.

Highlife and Afrobeat. Bright rippling chords, then tight punchy stabs. Let's groove.
Highlife comes from West Africa, from brass bands and guitar music. On keys, play rippling broken chords, like a guitar, over a bouncy bass. Bright and happy.
Afrobeat is one long groove, often on one minor chord. The keys play short, punchy chords between the beats, and leave gaps. The gaps are part of the rhythm.
Every instrument has its own little pattern, and they fit together like a puzzle. Play yours the same every time and listen to the bass.

Playing for a singer means making them sound great. Let's learn how.
When you play for a singer, your job is to make them sound good. Play an introduction, keep a steady beat, and follow them if they slow down.
Keep your right hand below the singer's notes. Play less while they sing, and fill a little in the gaps. Simple and steady is best.
Choose a pattern for the style. A ballad has gentle broken chords. A waltz goes bass, chord, chord. Slow gospel rolls in groups of three.

Let's find your voice. Listen to a note, then sing it back.
Stand or sit tall, with loose shoulders. Breathe in low and quietly, like smelling a flower, so your tummy gently grows. Never push or strain your voice.
Listen to the note first. Hum it quietly inside your head. Then sing it on loo or ah. Deeper voices can sing it lower. The app accepts any octave.
While you sing, a line shows your pitch. Green means right on. Amber means close. Red means off. If you are too low, think up. If you are too high, relax.
Next up, Match C, E, G, D. Sing each note back and hold it steady. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
Do, re, mi, fa, so. Let's sing the first five notes of the scale.
Do, re, mi, fa, sol are names for the steps of the scale. Do is home. Each one has its own feeling. Mi is bright. Sol is strong. Re wants to fall back to do.
All the steps here are small. Keep the sound smooth and connected, with one breath going up and one breath coming down.
Next up, Do to Sol and back no rush. Sing each step in turn. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
Next up, Do to Sol in time. Sing with the beat at 60 beats per minute. Press start. You will hear a count in, then play along with the click.
Now jump between notes, thirds and fifths.
Do to mi is a small jump. Do to sol is a bigger one. Before each jump, imagine the note in your head first, then sing it straight on, without sliding.
Next up, Do Mi Sol Mi Do. Leap cleanly to each note. Take your time. The music waits for you on every note.
